en: The Sūtra on Loyalty Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time,
The various bodhisattvas, the fourfold assembly of disciples, devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, and subjects gathered daily to hear the sutras.

On the Buddha’s right side was a bhikṣu named Maudgalyāyana, whose supernormal powers were wondrously perfected and whose wisdom was like space; he manifested transformations according to the occasion, employing both skillful means and wisdom to universally save beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such that all the devas bowed their heads in reverence, regarding him as their teacher and model.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"There is a great kingdom eight thousand [yojanas] from here, situated on the borderlands.

They do not behold the supreme sageliness of the Triple Gem, nor have they rarely heard of the Tathāgata—the one who is unattached, the Truly Real, the Perfectly Awakened One—nor of his divine and wondrous pure transformation. They practice inverted and manifold heterodox ways, regarding them as the ultimate truth."

The king, along with his ministers and subjects, served five hundred brahmins, each of whom possessed the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), having the strength to move mountains, arrest the flow of rivers, and manifest transformations by dividing their bodies.
The kingdom had a great mountain that blocked the paths of the people, causing distress throughout the entire land.
The king, considering the mountain a hardship for his subjects, related this matter in detail to the brahmin.
The brahmins replied, "We are merely removing a pest for the sake of the people; let the King have no anxiety!
They then sat encircling the mountain, each concentrating his mind, and by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they caused the mountain to rise up as if to move.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"Go to that country and manifest the divine transformations of the Way; bring long-term benefit to the brahmins, deliver their ruler and people, and cause them to distance themselves from the three miserable realms so they may dwell forever in the halls of merit."

Maudgalyāyana received these instructions and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, immediately emitted light along the path to obscure the brilliance of the sun; he suspended himself in mid-air directly above the mountain peak, yet the mountain remained unmoved.
The brahmin was startled and said:
"This mountain has already risen; who could turn it back?
Furthermore, the sun lacks its radiance; there must be a reason for this!"
Among them was one who possessed clear insight; with a concentrated mind, he observed the hearts of his many disciples to see which were defiled and turbid, and thus caused the mountain not to move.

Having perceived that all their minds were universally pure through the Way, radiant with the precious colors of national glory, and that their hearts were undefiled, [he allowed the mountain to shift].
Looking up, they beheld a śramaṇa upon the mountain peak.
The brahmins all said,
"This is surely the work of a disciple of Gautama."
The brahmin called out, saying, "The King has commanded us to remove the suffering of the people; why do you suppress it?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I have suspended myself in mid-air; who is suppressing your mountain?
The Brahmin exhausted his spiritual powers three times, wishing to move the mountain, but the mountain sank down three times until it finally became level ground.
The brahmins looked at one another and said,
"He who possesses clear understanding and profound virtue and morality is our teacher. They all rose,
adjusted their robes, and prostrated themselves, respectfully addressing him:
“We wish to become your disciples; please show us the ultimate holiness.
Maudgalyāyana replied, “If you wish to leave darkness and proceed toward light, it is well!”
"I have a venerable teacher, titled the Unsurpassed, Truly Righteous One, the God among Gods, who possesses all-knowledge.
You should follow me to where the Buddha is."
The brahmins asked,
"Is the Buddha’s guidance and transformation not different from that of our teacher?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"The Buddha takes Mount Sumeru to be a mustard seed, while I take a mustard seed to be Mount Sumeru.
Having finished extolling the Buddha's virtues, he said, "Follow after me."

Maudgalyāyana joined the various brahmins together, and in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, he was before the Buddha, fully recounting the circumstances and saying to the Buddha:

"I have received the transformation of the power of the Unsurpassed True and Divine One; I have transformed these brahmins, and they are now pure both internally and externally, like new cotton cloth that is easily dyed."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will wash away these subtle defilements and cause us to become truly pure.
Upon seeing the Buddha, the brahmins’ minds were opened and their hearts filled with joy; they all became śramaṇas.
The Buddha said:

"I have preached the sutra for you; its beginning is excellent, its middle is excellent, and its end is excellent. Within these words, I have expounded the profound Way of transcending the world, taking the rectification of the mind as its foundation."
"Listen to my words so that they may be transmitted and practiced by future generations.
All the bhikṣus joined their palms and received the instruction.
The Buddha said:
“Within the human body there are five thieves that lead people into the evil realms.
What are these five? First is form;
second is sensation; third is perception; fourth is volitional formations; and fifth is consciousness. These five are what people constantly contemplate.”
The Buddha said:
"A person is constantly deceived by the eyes, deceived by the ears, deceived by the nose, deceived by the mouth, and deceived by the body."
The eye can only see and cannot hear;
the ear can only hear and cannot see;
the nose can only perceive fragrance and stench and cannot perceive taste.
The mouth can only perceive flavors but cannot perceive fragrances or odors;
the body can only perceive coldness and warmth but cannot perceive flavors. These five [senses] all belong to the mind; the mind is the foundation.
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus! Those who seek the Way should rectify their minds."
Because people follow from ignorance, there is birth and death according to the twelve links of dependent origination.
What are these twelve links of dependent origination?

First is ignorance; second is volitional formations; third is consciousness; fourth is name-and-form; fifth is the six sense bases; sixth is contact; seventh is sensation; eighth is craving; ninth is grasping; tenth is becoming; eleventh is birth; and twelfth is death.
Those who practice good will again become human;
those who practice evil enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and spirits.
The Buddha sat in contemplation, reflecting that birth and death exist because of human folly.

"What is delusion? Originally arising from delusion, one is born again as a human being and remains deluded; the mind lacks understanding and the eyes lack clarity, such that one does not know where one shall go when death occurs."

To see the Buddha and not inquire after him; to see the sutras and not read them; to see śramaṇas and not serve them; to have no faith in the Way and its Virtue; to see one's parents and not revere them; to fail to contemplate the suffering of the world; and to be ignorant of the severe punishments and torments in hell—this is called delusion. Therefore, birth and death continue without ceasing.
Human death occurs in the space of a single breath; nothing is more fragile than human life.
Within the human body, there are three things that depart when the body dies:
consciousness departs, the mind departs, and the intellect departs.
These three always pursue one another.
Those who practice evil enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and spirits;
those who practice goodness are likewise pursued by these three, being reborn either in the heavens or among human beings.
"Those who fall into these five realms of existence do so because their minds are not upright.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"You must all make your eyes upright, your ears upright, your noses upright, your mouths upright, your bodies upright, and your minds upright. When your physical bodies have been severed from the earth, your spirits shall no longer fall into the hells, the animal realm, or among the ghosts and spirits."
When one observes that people have wicked sons who are seized by the officials, it is entirely because their hearts were not upright.
Within the human body there are a hundred characters, just as a chariot has a hundred names.

Most people are greedy for what is pleasant and prone to anger; they do not contemplate the affairs within their own bodies, and upon dying and entering hell, their subsequent regrets will be of no avail.

I have abandoned my kingdom and renounced the status of a Wheel-Turning King; desiring to sever the cycle of birth and death and to deliver the people of the world so that they may attain the Way of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), those who exert themselves with the highest diligence immediately attained Arhatship;
those who exerted themselves with the second level of diligence attained Anāgāminship.
The third who exerts diligence attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;
the fourth who exerts diligence attains the stage of Srotāpanna;
though they cannot exert great diligence, they should uphold the five precepts:
"Do not kill, do not steal, do not commit sexual misconduct, do not engage in double-tongued speech, and do not drink intoxicants.
The Buddha said:
"When a person is sitting or rising, they should constantly contemplate these four matters."
What are the four?
First, one contemplates one's own body and contemplates the bodies of others;
second, one contemplates one's own sensations and contemplates the sensations of others.
Third, one observes one’s own mind and observes the minds of others;
fourth, one observes one’s own phenomena and observes the phenomena of others.

If the internal mind is again disturbed, one should straighten the mind and observe the body: whether it is at the extreme of hunger or the extreme of satiety, at the extreme of walking or the extreme of standing, at the extreme of sitting, or at the extreme of cold or heat.
When one is about to lie down to sleep, one should startle oneself awake, sit up, and sit with a composed mind;
if the mind is not composed, one should stand up;
if one is not composed while standing, one should practice walking meditation.
If the mind is not upright, one should rectify it oneself.
It is like a king leading his army into battle: the brave ones go to the front;
once they have gone to the front, if they are base and retreat again, they will surely bring shame upon those behind them.

“O bhikṣus! Having abandoned the home and renounced wife and children, shaving off hair and beard to become śramaṇas, although you may undergo diligent hardship for a single lifetime, you shall later attain long-term liberation.”
Those who have already attained the Way rejoice inwardly and alone; they regard their wives as sisters or younger siblings and their children as friends, free from any heart of greedy attachment.

They should always maintain compassion for all the devas and humans of the ten directions, as well as those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and even the smallest crawling and flying insects, causing them all to become wealthy, noble, peaceful, and secure, and to attain liberation through the Way of Non-action.
Upon seeing insects or beasts, one should treat them with compassion and pity, knowing that they will no longer be deluded regarding their lives.
One who can maintain such an intention constantly remembers the kindness of their teacher and serves the Buddha as a person thinks of their parents;
it is like a wise person going to a prison to petition for the release of a prisoner condemned to death.

The wise always remember the kindness of the virtuous; a bhikṣu who has attained the Path should likewise bring the Buddha to mind. One should contemplate the Sūtra in this way, just as a person thinks of food and drink.

“Monks, you should serve one another in succession, as a younger brother serves an elder brother. Among you, those who are ignorant should question those who are wise, and you should instruct one another in turn.
Questioning the wise is like having a lamp in the darkness; do not plot evil in secret, and do not engage in disputes.”
One should regard gold and silver as one regards soil; do not falsely testify regarding others entering into sinful states, and in speech, do not falsely injure another's reputation.

If you have not heard something, do not say you have heard it; if you have not seen something, do not say you have seen it. When walking the path, one should keep the head lowered and look at the ground; do not trample and kill the insects upon the earth.
Do not fix your eyes upon women; do not dwell on their physical forms.
Sit in self-reflection and eliminate the mind of craving and attachment; only then can you attain the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those who seek the Way should rectify their minds and sit in a secluded place, observing their own inhalations and exhalations, and knowing whether the breath is short or long."
If one holds the breath for a long time without exhaling, the body becomes exhausted;
if one closes the breath and does not let it flow, the body likewise becomes exhausted.
Through analytical reflection, one considers: who is the creator of this body?
The mind should look within and also observe without.
When one reflects upon this with joy, realizing that one’s mind differs from that of others, at that moment one has no further use for the rare treasures of the world.
If the mind slightly inclines toward the right path but the intention wavers again, one should immediately return to guarding that intention; thus the intention is restored.
It is like a person who possesses a mirror: if the mirror is not clear, one cannot see one's reflection; only by polishing it to remove the grime can one see one's own form.
A person removes greed, anger, and delusion, just as one polishes a mirror.
They reflect upon themselves and realize that nothing in the world is solid or permanent; all things are devoid of constancy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"You should maintain the mind like a square stone. Suppose there is a stone in a courtyard; rain cannot destroy it, the sun's heat cannot dissolve it, and the wind cannot move it. You should maintain the mind just like that stone."
The Buddha said:
"The minds of people in the world are like grasses and trees in a flowing stream; each flows along on its own, without looking back at one another.
Those in front do not look back at those behind, and those behind do not look back at those in front. As the grasses and trees flow, each remains as it was."
The human mind is also like this: one thought comes and another thought goes, just as grasses and trees do not look back upon one another from moment to moment.
Within the heavens above and the earth below, there is nothing further to delight in; dwelling as a temporary guest between heaven and earth, one casts off the body and does not die again.

Only upon attaining the Way does one realize the teacher's kindness; seeing the teacher, one serves them, and not seeing them, one contemplates their instructions as a filial son thinks of his parents.
When the mind is settled, one gains single-mindedness, and thus feels compassion for all people in the world and even for the smallest of crawling and flying creatures.
Sitting alone, he sighed to himself that he had liberated his person from the world and the five destinies:
first, the destiny of gods; second, the destiny of humans; third, the destiny of animals; fourth, the destiny of hungry ghosts; and fifth, the destiny of hell-beings.
Those who have already attained the path of Arhatship are able to fly and manifest transformations.

They can emit water and fire from within their bodies; they can pass through solid barriers and enter into what has no openings. If they wish to depart from the world and proceed toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are immediately able to do so.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Path must be studied; the sūtras must be read.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sūtra, five hundred śramaṇas all attained the state of arhatship.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"How is it that these śramaṇas have so swiftly understood the meaning of the sutra upon hearing it?
The Buddha said:
"These bhikṣus received and recited this sutra during the time of the previous Kāśyapa Buddha;
in the interim, as no Buddha appeared, it was abandoned according to worldly conditions and was no longer heard. Now that I have come to preach it, they have attained the Way upon hearing it."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, the fourfold assembly of disciples, kings, officials, and commoners, as well as devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, were filled with joy and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sutra on Loyal Devotion Spoken by the Buddha
